dedupe_keys.name: crrel database of icing related communication tower failures in the united states

description: The US Army Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory built a database of collapses of communication towers caused by atmospheric icing in the United States, described by Nathan Mulherin in the journal Cold Regions Science and Technology in April 1998. It records failures of 140 towers from 1959 onward, including radio and television broadcast masts, microwave relay towers and two-way radio towers, with the date, place and conditions, such as freezing rain, rime or in-cloud icing, and wind. Mapping the failures shows where and when icing collapses happen, with most in a belt across the central and eastern states and in winter storms, and the paper discusses how ice load and wind on guys and antennas combine to bring towers down and what this means for design standards. Recent events, such as the collapse of several towers including a 630-foot FM tower at East Jordan, Michigan, in the March 2025 ice storm, show the hazard continues. Coverage: United States, 1959 to about 1996. Format and access: journal article with summary tables; the underlying database is held by CRREL and was not found online. Caveats: compiled from news and industry reports, so smaller failures are missed; not updated publicly since the paper. Simulation uses: fragility and failure frequency of tall towers under ice and wind for broadcast and telecom resilience models, and regional hazard exposure of transmitter networks. Related records: the monopole tower seismic fragility data cover another hazard, and the FCC antenna structure registration gives tower locations and heights.
